title: Doppler Effect and Sonic Booms
lead: The scream of a motorcycle drops to a roar as it passes, because the motion of a source or of an observer changes the frequency that is received. This section explains why the wavelength is shortened ahead of a moving source and lengthened behind it, gives the frequency an observer receives for a moving source and for a moving observer, and follows a source past the speed of sound, where its waves pile up into a sonic boom.
objectives: Define Doppler effect, Doppler shift, and sonic boom.
Calculate the frequency of a sound heard by someone observing Doppler shift.
Describe the sounds produced by objects moving faster than the speed of sound.
summary_html:
• The Doppler effect is an alteration in the observed frequency of a sound due to motion of either the source or the observer.
  • The actual change in frequency is called the Doppler shift.
  • A sonic boom is constructive interference of sound created by an object moving faster than sound.
  • A sonic boom is a type of bow wake created when any wave source moves faster than the wave propagation speed.
  • For a stationary observer and a moving source, the observed frequency $\kfobs$ is: $\kfobs = \kfsrc\left(\frac{\kvw}{\kvw \pm \kvs}\right),$ where $\kfsrc$ is the frequency of the source, $\kvs$ is the speed of the source, and $\kvw$ is the speed of sound. The minus sign is used for motion toward the observer and the plus sign for motion away.
  • For a stationary source and moving observer, the observed frequency is: $\kfobs = \kfsrc\left(\frac{\kvw \pm \kvobs}{\kvw}\right),$ where $\kvobs$ is the speed of the observer.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 17.13) Sounds emitted by a source spread out in spherical waves. Because the source, observers, and air are stationary, the wavelength and frequency are the same in all directions and to all observers. (Figure 17.14) Sounds emitted by a source moving to the right spread out from the points at which they were emitted. The wavelength is reduced and, consequently, the frequency is increased in the direction of motion, so that the observer on the right hears a higher-pitch sound. The opposite is true for the observer on the left, where the wavelength is increased and the frequency is reduced. (Figure 17.15) The same effect is produced when the observers move relative to the source. Motion toward the source increases frequency as the observer on the right passes through more wave crests than she would if stationary. Motion away from the source decreases frequency as the observer on the left passes through fewer wave crests than he would if stationary.

Sound waves from a source that moves faster than the speed of sound spread spherically from the point where they are emitted, but the source moves ahead of each. Constructive interference along the lines shown (actually a cone in three dimensions) creates a shock wave called a sonic boom. The faster the speed of the source, the smaller the angle θ.
Two sonic booms, created by the nose and tail of an aircraft, are observed on the ground after the plane has passed by.

exercises.prompt: Why did scientist Christian Doppler observe musicians both on a moving train and also from a stationary point not on the train?

answer.solution: Doppler needed to compare the perception of sound when the observer is stationary and the sound source moves, as well as when the sound source and the observer are both in motion.

exercises.prompt: Describe a situation in your life when you might rely on the Doppler shift to help you either while driving a car or walking near traffic.

answer.solution: If I am driving and I hear Doppler shift in an ambulance siren, I would be able to tell when it was getting closer and also if it has passed by. This would help me to know whether I needed to pull over and let the ambulance through.

exercises.prompt: A baggage handler stands on the edge of a runway as a landing plane approaches. Compared to the pitch of the plane as heard by the plane’s pilot, which of the following correctly describes the sensation experienced by the handler?

options: The frequency of the plane will be lower pitched according to the baggage handler and will become even lower pitched as the plane slows to a stop.
The frequency of the plane will be lower pitched according to the baggage handler but will increase in pitch as the plane slows to a stop.
The frequency of the plane will be higher pitched according to the baggage handler but will decrease in pitch as the plane slows to a stop.
The frequency of the plane will be higher pitched according to the baggage handler and will further increase in pitch as the plane slows to a stop.
answer.hint: The pilot moves with the source and hears $\kfsrc$ itself. The handler is a stationary observer of a source moving toward him, so the minus sign applies, and the shift grows with $\kvs$.

figure.alt: A graph of time in seconds on the x-axis versus perceived frequency in hertz on the y-axis. The line is flat at 218 hertz from 0 to about 0.5 seconds, then declines linearly from (0.5, 218) to (0.8, 181), and then is flat at 181 hertz until the line ends.
figure.caption: Plot of time versus perceived frequency to illustrate the Doppler effect.

exercises.prompt: The following graph represents the perceived frequency of a car as it passes a student. (a) If the true frequency of the car’s horn is 200 Hz, how fast was the car traveling? (b) On the graph above, draw a line demonstrating the perceived frequency for a car traveling twice as fast. Label all intercepts, maximums, and minimums on the graph.

answer.solution: The horn is a moving source and the student a stationary observer, so the two flat parts of the graph are the two readings of $\kfobs = \kfsrc\left(\frac{\kvw}{\kvw \pm \kvs}\right)$ with $\kfsrc = 200\ \text{Hz}$: 218 Hz while the car approaches, with the minus sign, and 181 Hz after it has passed, with the plus sign. For (a), solve either reading for the speed of the car. The approaching reading gives $\kvs = \kvw\left(1 - \frac{200\ \text{Hz}}{218\ \text{Hz}}\right) = 0.083\,\kvw$ and the receding reading gives $\kvs = \kvw\left(\frac{200\ \text{Hz}}{181\ \text{Hz}} - 1\right) = 0.105\,\kvw$; the two differ because the frequencies are read off a graph, so take a speed of sound of about 343 m/s and report a speed of roughly 30 m/s. The sloping part between 0.5 s and 0.8 s is the car going by, when its motion is no longer along the line to the student. For (b), a car twice as fast has twice the ratio $\kvs/\kvw$, about 0.17, so its line starts higher, near $200\ \text{Hz}/(1 - 0.17) \approx 240\ \text{Hz}$, and ends lower, near $200\ \text{Hz}/(1 + 0.17) \approx 170\ \text{Hz}$. The car covers the same stretch of road in half the time, so the sloping part of the new line is half as wide, running from 0.5 s to about 0.65 s, and both shifts are larger than before: the shift up is larger than the shift down, as the two equations require.

exercises.prompt: Is the Doppler shift real or just a sensory illusion?

answer.solution: It is real. Ahead of a moving source the compressions of the air really are closer together, because each one was emitted from a point farther along than the one before, so the wavelength in the air is shorter there and, since $\kvw = \kf\klam$ with $\kvw$ fixed by the medium, the frequency arriving at a stationary observer really is higher. An observer walking toward a stationary source really does meet more crests each second than one standing still. A microphone, a radar receiver or an ultrasound probe measures the shifted frequency just as an ear hears it, which is why the shift can be used to measure the speed of blood, cars and galaxies.

exercises.prompt: Due to efficiency considerations related to its bow wake, the supersonic transport aircraft must maintain a cruising speed that is a constant ratio to the speed of sound (a constant Mach number). If the aircraft flies from warm air into colder air, should it increase or decrease its speed? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: It should decrease its speed. The speed of sound in air depends on the temperature, $\kvw = (331\ \text{m/s})\sqrt{\kTemp/273\ \text{K}}$, so colder air carries sound more slowly. The Mach number is the ratio $\kvs/\kvw$ of the aircraft’s speed to the speed of sound, and to keep that ratio the same when $\kvw$ falls the aircraft must reduce $\kvs$ in the same proportion. The angle of its bow wake, which is set by that ratio, then stays the same.

exercises.prompt: When you hear a sonic boom, you often cannot see the plane that made it. Why is that?

answer.solution: The plane is moving faster than the sound it makes, so the shock wave trails behind it on a cone and reaches the ground only after the plane has passed overhead. By the time the boom arrives, the plane is well beyond the point where you would look for it, and the sound seems to come from where the plane was rather than from where it is. Figure 17.17 shows this: the observers hear the booms after the aircraft has gone by, and the one the shock wave has not yet reached hears nothing at all.

exercises.prompt: (a) What frequency is received by a person watching an oncoming ambulance moving at 110 km/h and emitting a steady 800-Hz sound from its siren? The speed of sound on this day is 345 m/s. (b) What frequency does she receive after the ambulance has passed?

parts.hint: Convert 110 km/h to meters per second first. The ambulance is a moving source coming toward a stationary observer, so use the minus sign in $\kfobs = \kfsrc\left(\frac{\kvw}{\kvw - \kvs}\right)$.
After it passes the source moves away, so the same equation takes the plus sign.

exercises.prompt: What frequency is received by a mouse just before being dispatched by a hawk flying at it at 25.0 m/s and emitting a screech of frequency 3500 Hz? Take the speed of sound to be 331 m/s.

answer.hint: The hawk is a source moving toward a stationary observer: $\kfobs = \kfsrc\left(\frac{\kvw}{\kvw - \kvs}\right)$.

exercises.prompt: A commuter train blows its 200-Hz horn as it approaches a crossing. The speed of sound is 335 m/s. (a) An observer waiting at the crossing receives a frequency of 208 Hz. What is the speed of the train? (b) What frequency does the observer receive as the train moves away?

parts.hint: Solve the moving-source equation with the minus sign for $\kvs$: $\kvs = \kvw\left(1 - \kfsrc/\kfobs\right)$.
Use the speed from (a) in the same equation with the plus sign.

exercises.prompt: Two eagles fly directly toward one another, the first at 15.0 m/s and the second at 20.0 m/s. Both screech, the first one emitting a frequency of 3200 Hz and the second one emitting a frequency of 3800 Hz. What frequencies do they receive if the speed of sound is 330 m/s?

parts.hint: The first eagle receives the second’s 3800 Hz screech. Both are moving toward each other relative to the air, so the observer factor takes the plus sign with $\kvobs = 15.0\ \text{m/s}$ and the source factor the minus sign with $\kvs = 20.0\ \text{m/s}$, as in part (b) of Example 17.4.
Now the second eagle is the observer at 20.0 m/s and the first the source at 15.0 m/s, screeching at 3200 Hz.

answer.solution: First eagle hears $4.23 \times 10^{3}\ \text{Hz}$. Second eagle hears $3.56 \times 10^{3}\ \text{Hz}$.
